title: How to Build a Modding Community Around Your Game
description: A step-by-step plan for opening your game to mods: pick a Workshop model, ship tools and docs, set content rules, host the files and keep modders engaged.
intro: A modding community grows when a game is easy to extend, mods are easy to find and install, and modders can see that the studio pays attention. Most of the work is done before the first mod appears: choosing how content gets into the game, releasing the tools your own team uses, writing clear content rules and picking a place to host the files. This guide walks through those decisions in order, using Valve's Steam Workshop documentation and the main third-party options as reference points.
key_takeaways: Decide first whether mods load freely or pass through your approval, because that shapes your tools, moderation and support load.
Releasing your own development tools does more for modding than any announcement.
Write a style guide and content rules before launch so rejections are not a surprise.
Pick a hosting route that fits your platforms; Steam Workshop is one, mod.io targets PC, console and mobile.
Plan how players install and manage mods, because broken load order drives support tickets.

sections.h2: Start by choosing how mods reach players
paras: The first design choice is control. Valve's documentation describes two main Steam Workshop models. In a ready-to-use Workshop, anyone can upload content and players can download it without curation. That suits larger volumes of items, mods or maps, simple or complex, and authors can update their work whenever they like. In a curated Workshop, the developer approves each item, which gives tight control but requires work and an update to add every item. Valve says that model is typically better for smaller pieces such as weapons or hats.

Match the model to your game. A sandbox or strategy game with deep systems benefits from the open model, because modders make total conversions and tools. A competitive shooter where balance matters may prefer curated cosmetics. You can also split: allow open mods for single-player content and curate anything that touches ranked play.

sections.h2: Ship your tools and data formats
paras: Modders can only extend what they can read and build. Valve's Workshop page advises that if you want large-scale modding, it is useful to release as much of your own development tools as possible, and says most moddable games have released their developer tools so authors can work with the same tools the studio used. Those tools can also validate submissions and restrict which files may be overwritten.

At minimum, expose data in readable formats, document the folder layout, and give modders a staging environment where they can test a mod before publishing. Valve notes that your game needs a way to load content from disk and that you will need a staging place for creators. Build that loader early, because retrofitting it into a shipped game is slow and bug-prone.

sections.h2: Write a modding kit people can start from
paras: A tool alone does not start a community; the first hour of a modder's experience does. Publish a getting-started page with a working example mod, a short list of supported file types and the commands for packaging and testing. Provide a sample project that adds one visible change, such as a new weapon or a map tweak, so a newcomer sees a result within minutes.

Keep the kit versioned. Mods break when the game updates, so publish a changelog that lists changes to data formats and scripting APIs. Give every release a version number and say which game build it targets, so authors and players can tell what works with what.

sections.h2: Set content rules and a style guide
paras: State what you want and what you will remove. Valve recommends creating a style guide and, potentially, guidelines about the kinds of content you are looking for and the kinds you do not want posted. Cover licensed material, adult content, hate speech, malware and anything that breaks your game's terms. Say who enforces the rules and how takedowns work.

Rules reduce arguments later. Publish an appeals route, even a simple form, so modders know a human reads complaints. If your game has ratings or regional restrictions, decide how mods are rated and what happens when a mod changes the rating of your game.

Steam Workshop is the default for Steam games. Valve's implementation guide says the Workshop is a system of back-end storage and front-end web pages for storing, organizing, sorting, rating and downloading content, that players subscribe to items and that they download through Steam. By default, applications are not enabled to be publicly visible in the Workshop. You choose a visibility state of Developers Only, Developers and Testers, Customers and Developers, or Everyone. To set it to Everyone, the Workshop checklist must be complete, which includes branding, title, description and at least one publicly visible item of content.

If you ship on several storefronts, a cross-platform provider may fit better. mod.io describes itself as a platform that lets developers support mods on PC, console and mobile, with an API, SDK and plugins for Unity, Unreal Engine and more. Community sites also play a role: ModWorkshop describes itself as a place to share and download mods for various games, and Nexus Mods runs its own mod manager, Vortex, which its repository says supports over 250 games. Compare options in our ranking of [UGC and modding platforms](/software/best-ugc-and-modding-platforms).

sections.h2: Launch checklist for a Steam Workshop
paras: These steps follow Valve's implementation guide in the order you will meet them.
list: Set the Steam Cloud quota in the app admin panel, because Workshop preview images are stored in Steam Cloud.
Enable ISteamUGC for file transfer on the Steam Workshop Configuration page.
Publish those settings through Prepare for Publishing and Publish to Steam.
Build the upload path, in game or as a separate tool, using ISteamUGC::CreateItem with your game's App ID, not the App ID of a separate editor.
Make the game read the user's subscribed items and load them from disk.
Complete the Workshop checklist, set visibility to the level you want and publish the change.
after: Test the whole loop with developer-only visibility first. Upload a mod, subscribe on a second account, start the game and confirm that the mod loads and that updates arrive.

sections.h2: Installation, load order and mod managers
paras: Many support problems come from mod conflicts. If your game supports several mods at once, decide how load order works and show it in game. Players on PC often use external managers. Mod Organizer 2 describes itself as a free and open source Windows mod manager that installs, enables, disables and organizes mods without changing the original game files, with profiles and load order tools. See our ranking of [mod managers for PC games](/software/best-mod-managers-for-pc-games) for the options.
Make your game friendly to those tools. Keep mod files separate from base files, avoid hard-coded paths and document the load rules. Players who can undo a mod safely will try more of them.

Decide early whether mods can be sold. Valve says that with the ready-to-use model, enabling the option to sell items is straightforward, and that Steam Workshop collects bank and tax information from authors, provides the user agreements and handles payment processing and tax withholding. Items sold in a curated model need an inventory service to track who can equip them and an in-game store, with pricing controlled by the developer.

Even if you do not sell mods, think about creator recognition: credits in the launcher, featured mods in patch notes, or community spotlights. Recognition costs little and keeps authors updating their work.

sections.h2: Keep the community alive after launch
paras: A modding scene needs steady signals. Appoint a community contact who answers modders on your forum or Discord, post a short monthly note about upcoming changes that affect mods and give early builds to a few trusted authors before major patches. Watch for breakage after each update and publish fixes or migration notes quickly. For the moderation side of an active community server, our guide on [moderating a Discord server](/guides/how-to-moderate-a-discord-server) covers the basics, and the [community management tools](/software/best-community-management-tools-for-game-studios) ranking lists software that helps studios track modder questions.

faqs.q: Do I have to use Steam Workshop to support mods?
faqs.a: No. Steam Workshop is one route and fits Steam games. Other options include cross-platform services such as mod.io, community sites, or hosting files yourself. The right pick depends on your storefronts, whether you need console support and how much moderation you can run in house.

Only if you can support them. Valve documents that Steam Workshop can collect author tax details and handle payments, but you still need clear rules, refund handling and moderation for disputes. Many studios start with free mods, learn what the community builds and add paid items later.

faqs.q: How do I stop mods from breaking after updates?
faqs.a: You cannot prevent it fully, but you can reduce it. Keep data formats stable, publish a changelog before every patch, give modders a beta branch, and version your modding API. Tag each mod release with the game build it targets so players can match them.

faqs.q: What content rules do I need on day one?
faqs.a: Cover legality, licensed material, adult and hateful content, malware and the right to remove mods. Valve recommends a style guide and guidelines on the content you want and do not want. Add a way to report mods and an appeals route, and say who reviews reports.

faqs.q: How big does a game need to be before modding makes sense?
faqs.a: There is no threshold. Small games with readable data and simple scripting can attract modders, while large games with locked formats often cannot. What matters more is whether your tools and documentation let a motivated player make a change in an evening.
